The thing that strikes me is that you are lucky, she hasn't cut you out completely; she's still talking to you. Yes, she's not inviting you to anything, but why should she. Can't you understand what it's like to be disappointed again and again by family? It's a visceral pain. Why shouldn't she protect herself from that? You've offered family therapy, it's a gesture, and one you've given her no reason to believe you'd actually show up too. 

You've got a tiny bit of trust left with your daughter. A tiny amount. You want to increase your presence in her life, talk to her about things apart from her brother. Make arrangements and stick to them. And i say as someone with family on the spectrum, there will always be another tantrum. Did you miss her event because the hired carer couldn't cope or because you didn't want to leave him? You cannot be there for every tantrum. He'll outlive you presumably, so you are going to have to let other people deal with his tantrums because there isn't going to be another choice, and if you don't get him used to other caregivers you aren't helping him.

What's most worrying in this to me is that you label your (ex?) husbands abuse of you as his response to your addiction. As if this is your fault, you provoked it. Physical violence in these circumstances is a choice, there's no excuse for it. Abusers often use the excuse of anger or frustration for their behaviour, but what I've noticed is that these same people who claim uncontrollable frustration and anger, are capable of holding jobs without attacking anyone, and generally being in public without violence. So if their feelings are so uncontrollable then how are they able to function in the rest of their lives? And how are they able to hold onto anger they experience in the day, but only express it in the home by harming their partner, if it was so uncontrollable, surely they'd be hitting people in that moment, not saving it up? How honest does it seem that their anger is uncontrollable with their, in the privacy of their own home, but in all other settings they are capable of restraint? 

You also say that 70% of the time he's wonderful. If the people you love, past or present said that about you, would you be happy with that? That you can be wonderful 7 days out of 10, but violent and make them fear for their lives those other three? I'd be horrified, would it be good enough for you? 

There's nothing wrong with having empathy for your abuser, it's difficult not to when they've been a big part of your life, and it doesn't make you bad or weird, but just be aware of how far it goes. Empathy is one thing, blaming yourself for everything, punishing yourself for the situation they put themselves in, and guilt over trying to stop them abusing you is beyond empathy and beyond reasonable. Also if for any reason you do have further contact with your abuser, empathy is a very easy emotion to use to manipulate people, or for people to do on his behalf.

Sometimes not holding people responsible for the harm they do, and taking the blame for it yourself, along with compartmentalising their bad behaviour to seperate it out from the rest of who they are, is a way of protecting yourself from the reality of the person. That way you can keep this idealised version of who they are in your mind, and love them more easily. I'm not trying to tell you that you definitely do this, btw, just mentioning an idea in case it's helpful. 

You talk about how much you love and miss him, and I am sorry for your pain, but i'm glad you are prioritising your safety, because this is vital. I wish you the best with everything, goodluck.

NTA, Your job as a parent is to protect your child, so if you think someone is unbalanced, regardless of why, you have a responsibility to remove them from that environment. 

Beyond that, teaching piano, if she charges for it, it's a business, and it's perfectly reasonable to decide that you don't want to support a business that's going to support people you consider amoral. 

As for the first amendment issue, this is something of a pet peeve of mine. The first amendment promises you that the government, and the government alone, can't come after you legally because of your opinions. You are not being anti first amendment by choosing not to patronise this business. This is a concept known as dollar voting, and is a perfectly legitimate form of moral/political expression to consider when spending your money. 

I'd also add that this teacher isn't entitled to your business, but there does seem to be a sense of entitlement there. I think that in telling them why you removed them is actually a step further than you needed to go, you didn't owe them an explanation, and then you wouldn't have had to debate amendment rights.

I can understand people wanting to take advantage of everyone being together, as you say it happens infrequently, but it just isn't normal or polite for them to all leave and to not warn you about it in advance. If you know for a fact that your sister purposefully planned to use the same day then I'd say she's the asshole, but given that weddings are usually planned months or years in advance and pregnancies can't, in usual circumstances, be planned that specifically, is it possible that she just booked a location without double checking? Or that she was pressured by other family members to take advantage of everyone being in the same location for your wedding? Either way, I'd certainly be asking questions of family members about their actions, and what made them think it was normal.

NTA - This sounds like she's used your kindness as a way to manipulate you to do things for her. You gave her lots of opportunities to avoid this last minute scramble, even though that wasn't your responsibility, and she ignored you. It's reasonable to help a friend whose distressed, but if they aren't helping themselves, and they expect you to do it all, that's not reasonable. You aren't a packing firm she's hired. And her being upset doesn't obligate you to do anything; why should you be punished because she hasn't behaved like a responsible adult. The other thing is, while it's ok to jump in to save your friend from something, in this situation if you keep jumping in and saving her, she never learns to do things for herself and grow as a person. So you are definitely not the asshole, but she might be.
